props.title: Shark Tale
props.initialSlug: Little fish's big lie turns him into ocean legend

sections.content: Shark Tale (2004) marked DreamWorks Animation's attempt to capitalize on the success of Finding Nemo (2003), but took a drastically different approach by setting its story in an underwater urban environment styled after New York City. The film's use of celebrity voices - particularly Will Smith as Oscar and Robert De Niro as Don Lino - heavily influenced its marketing and character designs, creating fish characters that deliberately resembled their voice actors. This trend of celebrity-influenced character design became increasingly common in animated features, seen later in films like Madagascar (2005) and Megamind (2010).

sections.content: The film's portrayal of mob culture through aquatic life created an unusual mashup of genres, directly referencing classics like The Godfather (1972) and Goodfellas (1990). This approach of parodying adult-oriented films in family entertainment became a signature move for DreamWorks Animation, later seen in Shrek (2001) and Monsters vs. Aliens (2009). However, the film's reliance on pop culture references and adult-oriented jokes marked a distinct contrast to Pixar's more emotionally grounded storytelling approach. SUBHEAD: Animation Technology and Style

Shark Tale represented a significant technical achievement in underwater animation, though its stylistic choices favored urban realism over marine biology accuracy. The film's character designs prioritized anthropomorphic features and celebrity likenesses over aquatic authenticity, contrasting sharply with the more naturalistic approach of Finding Nemo (2003). This artistic decision influenced later underwater animated features like The Reef (2006) and Surf's Up (2007), which similarly balanced realism with stylized character design.
